dataIdInfo.idAbs: This is a polygon data set representing Boise Parks and Recreation data. A park is generally an area of land in a largely natural state, sometimes with grass, trees, paths, sports fields, playgrounds, picnic areas and other facilities, that is set aside and managed specifically for recreation use and enjoyment by the public. The features included in this polygon feature class are; parks, reserves, city maintained cemeteries, city maintained road rights-of-ways and greenbelt areas. This data set was created from a combination of Boise Parks and Recreation park and facility files and the Ada County Parcel records. This dataset was created by POWER Engineer's, Inc. and will be maintained by the City of Boise. This data set is updated at the request of Boise Parks and Recreation staff as changes to the park data occur. It is current to the date it was published.
dataIdInfo.idPurp: The National Parks and Recreation Association (NRPA) GIS Data Model was developed for jurisdictions to be able to inventory lands and assets that they own, plan, manage, operate and maintain. By providing standard attributes and values, the GIS Model makes it possible for better local, regional, and statewide management and planning of park and recreation resources. Locally relevant fields from the NRPA GIS model are used in this dataset. A number of other non-NRPA fields were created as well to meet more specific needs of Boise Parks and Recreation. BPR_Sites features identify areas of Boise Parks and Recreation maintained lands. The features include parks, city maintained road rights-of-way, reserves, and other city maintained areas. Boise Parks and Recreation determines which feature type they desire to portray each of the parks they manage. This data set was created for the Boise Parks and Recreation to meet the following needs: 1) general mapping of Boise Parks and Recreation amenities; 2) to manage Boise Parks and Recreation Department assets; 3) use in the Boise Parks and Recreation Comprehensive Plan, a long range plan for park improvements. To view details about the Comprehensive plan please visit citofboise.org/departments/parks.

LegConsts.useLimit: The information depicted in this GIS layer is the result of digital analysis performed on information from a variety of governmental and other credible sources. Accuracy is limited to the collective accuracy of the source data on the date of the analysis. The information is believed to be accurate and reasonable efforts have been made to ensure the accuracy of the data. However, the City of Boise expressly disclaims responsibility for damages or liability that may arise from use of this data.
LegConsts.othConsts: There are no restrictions to access for this data; the data is available to the general public. Any use of this data implies acceptance of the City of Boise's disclaimer and distribution liability statements.

Consts.useLimit: This data may be redistributed provided the following criteria are met: 1) if the data is unaltered then the complete City of Boise metadata for this data set must accompany the data; or 2) if the data is altered in any way prior to redistribution, the City of Boise metadata will not be included and the redistributors will reference City of Boise as a source of the data.

dataIdInfo.suppInfo: Parcel data is managed by the Ada County Assessor's Office, therefore the original source for parcel data is the Ada County Assessor's Office. Park data is based on parcel data but is not a 1-1 link. A park may be made up of one or more parcels or parts of parcels or lie outside of parcel areas in the rights-of way. The Ada County parcel data is referenced as a base but the park data are separate entities. Where park areas follow Ada County parcels exactly, the Ada County Parcel(s) was used to build the park polygon. Where park maintained areas do not follow any parcel line the park area was digitized from the Ada County orthophotography (multiple years, starting in 2007).

edom.edomvd: Neighborhood sites serve people living within an approximately 0.5- to 1-mile radius. They are generally 5 to 10 acres in size and often located adjacent to or near public school properties.
These sites serve populations of 7,500 to 15,000 living within a service area of approximately 1- to 2-mile radius. These sites are generally 10 to 30 acres in size.
Special-use sites are intended to provide single-purpose dedicated park facilities for specialized recreational programs, services, and activities. These sites serve the entire community.

Large urban sites are designed to serve the entire community. Generally, they provide a wide variety of specialized facilities. They usually exceed 50 acres in size and should be designed to accommodate large numbers of people.
Regional sites are recreational areas that serve the City and area beyond. They are usually large and include one specific use or feature that makes the site unique.
This covers areas maintained by Parks and Recreation that fall within road rights-of-way, including medians and islands.
Mini-parks, tot lots, children's playgrounds, and community gardens are single-purpose properties offering a limited range of passive or active recreational uses.
Open space reserves are the City's largest parkland holdings. These areas are highly valued for their passive recreational values and natural and cultural resources.
An area that generally falls in a corridor along waterfront, trails or areas connecting parks.

What constitutes an open space according to COMPASS: land that is highly unlikely to be developed because of an easement, ownership, or prescriptive use. Parks, golf courses, cemeteries all fall within this category, as does public agency owned land with either a defined use such as wildlife habitat or land designated multiple use.
